common_name: Monsella Tulip (Yellow Double Early Tulip Flamed Red)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6-8 inches deep in well-drained soil in fall; the fully double flower form means each bulb produces a much fuller, peony-like bloom than a single-form tulip.

directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained soil in full sun in fall for an early-to-mid-spring display. Monsella's fully double, bowl-shaped flowers open canary yellow with cherry-red flame markings that intensify as the bloom ages, giving a peony-like fullness unusual for an early tulip. Because the heavy double blooms sit lower and sturdier than lily-flowered types, Monsella holds up well in exposed containers and borders without staking. It is also lightly fragrant, a trait many double early tulips share.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in fall; this 1986 hybrid is considered by many bulb growers to be the finest large all-yellow trumpet daffodil available.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Marieke produces huge, upward-facing, pure golden-yellow blooms with a wide, ruffled trumpet, and the color holds its richness with unusual staying power as the flower ages rather than fading or bleaching in sun. It is an exceptionally floriferous naturalizer and a favorite for indoor forcing because of its reliable, vigorous performance. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after bloom so the bulb recharges for next year's display.

common_name: Fellows Favorite Daffodil (Fragrant Large-Cup Yellow Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in well-drained soil in fall; this classic Division 2 large-cup daffodil has been a garden standard for decades.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun. Fellows Favorite opens a brilliant greenish-yellow and gradually develops a white-banded base as the long, funnel-shaped cup matures to a richer yellow-orange, giving the bloom a two-tone look as it ages on the plant. The flowers carry a light, sweet fragrance that is noticeable even in open garden settings, not just indoors as a cut flower. It is a vigorous, reliable naturalizer well suited to mass plantings in borders and under deciduous trees.

common_name: Golden Echo Daffodil (Fragrant Jonquilla Daffodil with Yellow Halo)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in fall; this Jonquilla hybrid carries multiple fragrant blooms per stem rather than the single flower typical of trumpet types.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Golden Echo carries up to three fragrant white-petaled blooms in a triangular cluster on each stem, each centered with a bright yellow cup that creates a glowing halo effect against the white perianth. As a jonquilla type it is more heat-tolerant and reliably perennial in warmer zones than many trumpet or large-cup daffodils, naturalizing readily in borders and lawns. Deer and rodents generally leave it alone, making it a low-maintenance choice for mixed bulb plantings.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall; in warm-winter zones (9+), pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator 6-8 weeks before planting since hyacinths require a cold period to flower properly.

directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in full to partial sun in fall. Aida produces dense, tightly packed flower spikes in a deep violet-blue that reads almost indigo in cooler light, with the same intensely sweet, heavy fragrance that makes hyacinths prized as both garden and forced indoor bulbs. The glossy, strap-like foliage stays attractively compact and does not flop the way some large-flowered hyacinths can. A single forced stem is often enough to perfume an entire room.

common_name: Gypsy Queen Hyacinth (Fragrant Salmon-Peach Heirloom Hyacinth)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall; in warm-winter zones (9+), pre-chill bulbs in the refrigerator 6-8 weeks before planting since hyacinths require a cold period to flower properly.

directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in full to partial sun in fall. Gypsy Queen is an heirloom hyacinth with an unusual soft salmon-peach color brightened by buttery-yellow highlights, a shade that stands apart from the more common blues, pinks, and whites in the hyacinth palette. Its intense, sweet fragrance carries just as strongly as other hyacinth cultivars despite its more delicate coloring. It performs equally well in garden borders, containers, and as a forced indoor bulb for late-winter bloom.

common_name: Tinkerbelle Lilac (Dwarf Spicy-Fragrant Reblooming Pink Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; this dwarf hybrid of Syringa meyeri and S. microphylla stays far more compact than common lilac.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in spring. Tinkerbelle opens deep wine-red buds that unfurl into five-inch panicles of pink flowers carrying the classic lilac scent with an added spicy note, a fragrance distinct enough to stand out even among other reblooming lilac introductions. Bred by crossing two dwarf Asian lilac species, it keeps a dense, rounded habit without the suckering and legginess of common lilac, making it a good fit for smaller landscapes. Light deadheading after the main spring flush can encourage a modest rebloom later in the season.

common_name: Sugar Plum Fairy Lilac (Compact Fragrant Rosy-Pink Fairytale Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; this is the most compact member of the Fairytale series of dwarf lilacs.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in spring. Sugar Plum Fairy blooms later than most common lilac cultivars, bearing frothy, spicy-scented panicles of soft rosy-pink flowers that extend the lilac season into early summer. Its compact, dense habit stays tidy without heavy pruning, making it one of the easier dwarf lilacs to work into a foundation planting or mixed shrub border. The strong fragrance and extended bloom window make it a favorite for gardeners who want lilac scent after the classic varieties have already finished.

common_name: Betsy Ross Lilac (Early Reblooming Pure White Lilac)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; this U.S. National Arboretum introduction blooms earlier than common lilac and can produce a light rebloom later in the season.

directions: Plant in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun in spring. Betsy Ross produces abundant, fragrant panicles of pure white single flowers that open earlier in the season than many common lilac cultivars, giving an extended lilac display when paired with later-blooming types. It was developed as part of a U.S. National Arboretum breeding program aimed at improving disease resistance and bloom reliability over older white lilac selections. The shrub forms a full, rounded habit and benefits from removing a few of the oldest stems at ground level every few years to keep flowering vigorous.

common_name: Hot Blooded Lantana (Sterile Gold-to-Red Compact Lantana)

planting.note: Plant container stock after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Hot Blooded is a sterile selection, so it sets no seed and channels all its energy into continuous bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun after the last frost; treat as a heat- and drought-tolerant annual outside zones 9-11. Hot Blooded's rounded flower clusters open golden yellow and deepen through fiery orange to a brilliant red as they age, so a single cluster often displays all three colors at once. Because it is bred sterile and sets no seed, it keeps producing new flower clusters all season instead of slowing down to ripen fruit, and its compact, well-branched habit suits containers, hanging baskets, and border edges. It draws butterflies and hummingbirds reliably through summer heat that stalls many other bedding plants.

common_name: Greyzini Zucchini (AAS-Winning Gray-Green Mottled Summer Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; thin to final spacing once seedlings have true leaves.

directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once danger of frost has passed. Greyzini produces straight, medium-green zucchini fruit lightly flecked and mottled with gray, a distinctive hybrid-vigor cross between green and golden zucchini types that earned it an All-America Selections award. The compact bush habit and early, heavy fruit set make it a dependable choice for small-space vegetable gardens, and fruit stays firm and non-seedy if picked at 6-8 inches. Harvest every day or two during peak season to keep plants productive.

common_name: Hubbard Essex Red Squash (Heirloom Warty Orange-Red Winter Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills or rows after soil has warmed; this vigorous vining heirloom needs ample room to sprawl through the season.

directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile soil in full sun once the danger of frost has passed, giving vines plenty of room to spread. Hubbard Essex Red, discovered in 1883 as a natural cross of Turban and Hubbard squash in Essex, Massachusetts, produces large, drum-shaped, deeply warty fruit with bright orange-red skin and sweet, dense orange flesh prized for pies and baking. Like other hubbard types it stores exceptionally well in a cool, dry spot through much of the winter once properly cured. Cure fruit in the sun for a week or two after harvest to toughen the rind before long-term storage.

common_name: Buffy Pepper (AAS-Winning Compact Ornamental Cayenne-Type Hot Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Buffy's upright, heavily fruited plants also work well in containers brought indoors over winter.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Buffy is a compact, upright AAS-winning pepper that sets an exceptionally heavy load of slender, two-inch fruit along its branches, ripening from dark green to glossy lipstick-red with real ornamental impact in beds or edible landscaping. It carries noticeable heat and cures quickly on the plant, making it well suited to drying or pickling as well as fresh use. The sturdy, deer- and disease-resistant plants hold up to heat stress better than many cayenne-type peppers.

common_name: Roulette Habanero Pepper (AAS-Winning Heatless Habanero-Flavor Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; habanero types are slow to germinate and benefit from consistently warm soil.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun well after the last frost. Roulette delivers the fruity, citrusy flavor of a classic habanero pepper in thick-walled, dark red fruit, but with almost none of the characteristic heat, making it an AAS-winning option for cooks who want habanero flavor without the burn. Its productive, well-branched plants hold fruit upright for easy harvest and good air circulation. Because it has so little capsaicin, this variety is also a reasonable choice for gardeners who want to introduce kids or heat-sensitive cooks to habanero flavor.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this disease-resistant hybrid sets fruit heavily on compact, 3-foot plants.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Emerald Fire sets heavy yields of extra-large, glossy, thick-walled jalapenos that resist cracking even as they mature from green to red, an AAS-winning improvement over older jalapeno types prone to splitting. The thick flesh holds up especially well to stuffing and grilling, while the compact, disease-resistant plants stay productive over a long harvest window. Pick at the deep green stage for classic jalapeno heat and crunch, or let fruit ripen to red for a sweeter, slightly milder flavor.

common_name: Rodina Beet (Smooth Cylindrical No-Thin Red Beet)

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep in loose, stone-free soil 2-4 weeks before last frost; the smooth cylindrical roots slice into uniform rounds.

directions: Direct sow in loose, fertile soil in full sun as soon as the ground can be worked in spring. Rodina produces long, smooth, tubular roots with a dark red color and blunt end, a shape that yields uniform slices from end to end and makes it a favorite for pickling and processing. Its dark green tops are notably slow to bolt and show good tolerance to common leaf diseases, so plantings stay productive longer into summer heat than many round beet types. Because the roots size up evenly along their length, successive sowings give a steady, predictable harvest for fresh eating or canning.

common_name: Wrinkle in Time Hosta (Ruffled Gold-Edged Dwarf Hosta)

planting.note: Plant bare-root crowns or container stock in spring or early fall into humus-rich, moist soil in part to full shade; this sport arose spontaneously from 'Pilgrim' at a Michigan nursery in 2010.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in part to full shade. Wrinkle in Time forms a small, dense clump of narrow green leaves edged in a creamy-yellow border so intensely wavy and rippled that the margin seems to be in constant motion, an effect that calms slightly in summer heat before the ruffling returns the following spring. Purple flowers rise on scapes above the foliage in late spring, though the foliage display is the main draw. Its compact size suits containers, patio edges, and the front of a shaded border where its texture can be appreciated up close.

common_name: Silly String Hosta (Narrow Wavy Blue-Green Dwarf Hosta)

planting.note: Plant bare-root crowns or container stock in spring or early fall into moderately fertile, moist soil in light shade; a 2022 Hans Hansen introduction bred from 'Curly Fries.'

directions: Grow in moderately fertile, moist, well-drained soil in light to full shade. Silly String forms a tangled, cascading mound of long, narrow, exaggeratedly wavy leaves that emerge a striking blue and settle into blue-green as the season progresses, giving the clump an almost tousled, textural look unlike broader-leaved hosta types. Pale purple flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. Its small size and urban tolerance make it a strong choice for border edges, containers, and filling in over fading spring bulb foliage.

common_name: Aromatico Blue Lavender (Compact Violet-Blue English Lavender)

planting.note: Transplant vegetatively propagated starts after last frost into sharply drained, lean to neutral soil in full sun; this Syngenta Flowers series selection is bred for uniform, early flowering.

directions: Transplant into sharply drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, since lavender resents wet feet. Aromatico Blue produces masses of fragrant violet-blue flower spikes over attractive gray-green, silver-tinged foliage, blooming from late spring through late summer with a tidy, uniform habit bred for container and landscape use. Its needle-like leaves take on a coppery-bronze tint in fall, adding late-season interest after flowering slows. Once established, it tolerates heat and drought well and needs little more than a light shearing after the main bloom flush to stay compact.
